title: Lhabab Duchen again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kathina, and Visakha noticing monks standing in the rain. Your line: the rains end in gifts.

What do you owe the person who gave birth to you? People answer with flowers, phone calls, money, or a seat at the head of the table. The Buddha's own story has a strange shape here. Tradition says his mother, Maya, died soon after his birth, so he never had the chance to repay her in the ordinary ways. After his awakening, the story goes, he went up to the heaven where she had been reborn, and spent a rains retreat teaching her. Then he came down. In Tibet, the day of that descent is Lhabab Duchen. You've met the staircase of the gods before. Today, ask why he went up at all.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU OWE YOUR MOTHER?` → `HE NEVER KNEW HER.` → `WHY DID HE GO UP?`

segments.voice: A debt that can't be paid. In the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha says there are two people you can never fully repay: your mother and your father. Even if you carried one on each shoulder for a long life, washed and fed them, and made them rulers of the earth, it wouldn't be enough. They brought you up, fed you, and showed you this world. Then the discourse turns to the one way it can be repaid. If your parents lack faith, you help them toward faith. If they lack virtue, toward virtue. If they're stingy, toward generosity. If they lack wisdom, toward wisdom. That, it says, repays them. Read Lhabab Duchen beside that discourse, and the trip to heaven looks like a son repaying a debt. He didn't bring his mother gold. He brought her the best thing he had, the teaching. Last, the coming down. When the season ended, he didn't stay. Tradition says he descended at Sankassa, to crowds waiting below. In Tibet, Lhabab Duchen is kept with offerings, circling holy places, and giving. Elsewhere, at the end of the rains, the same descent is remembered with alms rounds. He went up to honor one person and came back down for everyone. Some readers see in that the whole shape of the path: go deep for someone you love, then return to the ordinary crowd.
screen: `A DEBT YOU CAN'T REPAY.` · `UNLESS YOU HELP THEM GROW.` · `HE BROUGHT HER THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `HE CAME DOWN.`

segments.voice: Let your mother come to mind, or whoever mothered you, a grandmother, an aunt, a father who did both jobs, a foster parent, a teacher; if that relationship is painful, choose someone else who cared for you, or simply rest with the breath. Breathe in and remember one thing they made, carried or fixed for you; breathe out and let a little thanks go toward them, living or gone. If missing someone feels heavy today, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.
Lhabab Duchen. The Tibetan holy day of the Buddha's descent from heaven, after teaching his mother. Today's word.
Your line: he came down. Underneath the festival, a son and his mother. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: On Lhabab Duchen, Tibetan Buddhists visit temples, make offerings, recite prayers and mantras, circle stupas and holy places, and give generously; in Theravada lands the descent is remembered with alms rounds at the end of the rains.

chat.says: Why did the Buddha go up to heaven? What was he doing there?
options: Tradition says he taught his mother, repaying her with the best thing he had.
He went to be crowned king of the gods before returning to the earth.
He went to rest after his awakening, far away from the crowds below.
chat.meaning: The Buddha says parents are repaid by helping them toward faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom; tradition says he went up and taught his mother.

Maya.meaning: the Buddha's mother, who tradition says died soon after his birth

Lhabab Duchen.meaning: the Tibetan holy day of the Buddha's descent

Sankassa.meaning: where tradition says he came down from heaven

Numbered Discourses.meaning: a Pali collection of teachings, arranged by number

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary (the twin miracle and the descent at Sankassa)

notes: AN 2.33 (numbering varies, AN 2.31–32 in some editions) paraphrased: one parent on each shoulder for a hundred years ('a whole long life' in the voice), anointing, bathing, ruling the earth, still not repaid; establishing them in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom repays them. 'His mother, Maya, died soon after his birth': tradition gives seven days; the number is left out per the claims rule.
